passage:
Class 6 science, observation note, 14 August
Harish has not raised his hand once this term. In group discussions he watches, pencil still. I had filed him in my head as 'not interested'. Then I read his monsoon worksheet: a full page on why his grandfather's well fills late, with a drawing of the water table I had never taught. I felt a little ashamed of my assumption. Today I set up a question box where anyone can post a written question or answer after class. Harish posted two. At lunch I asked him, one to one, about the well. He talked for five minutes, eyes bright. Next week: written exit slips for everyone, and a short chat with each quiet student.
Mahima, class teacher

qa.q: What did Harish write about on the monsoon worksheet?
qa.a: Why his grandfather's well fills late, with a drawing of the water table.

qa.q: How did Mahima feel after reading Harish's worksheet?
qa.a: Mahima felt a little ashamed of having filed Harish as 'not interested' just because he was silent.

qa.q: Which of Mahima's changes suits Harish, and why?
qa.a: The question box and one-to-one chats, because they give him a written or private route to show what he knows.

qa.q: What was it like for Harish to be asked about the well at lunch?
qa.a: He seemed interested and happy, talking for five minutes with bright eyes once it was just the two of them.

grounding: Shows, in a teacher's note, a silent pupil whose written work reveals real interest, and the written and one-to-one routes offered to him.

passage:
Thursday night
Kamal again today. Eleven years old, back row, never a word. When I asked the class what makes a good friend, thirty hands went up and his stayed flat on the desk. I'll be honest, diary: I felt irritated. Then I collected the paragraphs. His was the best in the class. 'A good friend notices when you have gone quiet and doesn't make it a big thing.' I read it three times in the staffroom. Is he telling me what he needs? Tomorrow I'll try Mrs. Bose's idea: sticky notes on every desk, everyone writes one answer, and I read some out without names. And I'll ask Kamal to stay two minutes after the bell, just to tell him that sentence was beautiful.
Pooja

qa.q: What did Kamal write about a good friend?
qa.a: 'A good friend notices when you have gone quiet and doesn't make it a big thing.'

qa.q: How did Pooja feel when Kamal's hand stayed flat, and how did that change?
qa.a: Pooja felt irritated at first, then moved, reading his paragraph three times after finding it the best in the class.

qa.q: Why might the sticky-note plan help Kamal?
qa.a: Everyone writes an answer and some are read without names, so Kamal can share his thinking without having to speak up.

qa.q: How might Kamal feel when told after the bell that his sentence was beautiful?
qa.a: He would probably feel surprised and quietly proud, noticed without a fuss, just as his own sentence describes.

grounding: Shows a teacher who notices that a silent pupil writes the most thoughtful answer, and plans written and one-to-one routes for him.

passage: In the one-room school above the village in Lahaul, Dolma Madam held an oral quiz every Friday. The children shouted answers; the stove crackled. Ira, nine, sat by the window and never said a word. Dolma had begun to wonder whether the girl was bored, or unhappy at home. This Friday she walked the aisle and glanced down. Ira's slate was full: every answer right, and beside the river question a tiny map of the stream behind her house, with an arrow to the Chandra. Dolma felt warm, and a little foolish. After the quiz she knelt by Ira's desk. 'Will you be my slate answerer? You write, and show only me.' Ira nodded, and held her slate a little higher all afternoon.

qa.q: What did Ira draw beside the river question?
qa.a: A tiny map of the stream behind her house, with an arrow to the Chandra.

qa.q: What did Dolma Madam feel when she saw Ira's slate?
qa.a: She felt warm and a little foolish, having wondered whether Ira was bored or unhappy when she was quietly answering everything.

qa.q: Why is the 'slate answerer' idea a good route for Ira?
qa.a: It lets Ira show what she knows in writing, privately to the teacher, without having to shout in front of everyone.

qa.q: How might Ira feel holding the slate a little higher?
qa.a: Ira probably feels quietly proud and more confident, noticed in a way that suits her.

grounding: Shows a teacher discovering that a silent pupil knows every answer and offering her a written, private way to show it.

passage: Arnab, you think I don't understand why you can't stay home one Saturday? At sixteen your Hafsa Khala was a girl just like you. In Kolkata I said yes to every plan: cricket on the maidan, every wedding, every adda at the tea stall. An empty Sunday made me feel like a switched-off fan. One Puja night my crowd went up to a friend's terrace. Music, laughter, everyone daring each other to sit on the parapet for a photo, four floors up. I was next. They were chanting my name, and I wanted them to keep liking me more than I wanted anything. Then I looked down. I said, 'No. I'm going home.' They booed. Two of them walked me down anyway, and I told my father that night; by morning the terrace door had a lock. I still loved crowds, Arnab. I just stopped letting them choose for me.

qa.q: What were Hafsa's friends daring each other to do?
qa.a: To sit on the parapet of a terrace four floors up for a photo.

qa.q: What was Hafsa feeling as everyone chanted her name?
qa.a: Hafsa felt a strong pull to please them, wanting to be liked more than anything, with fear rising as she looked down.

qa.q: What turning point in Hafsa's story mattered most, and why?
qa.a: Looking down and saying 'No, I'm going home'; Hafsa chose safety over the crowd's approval, and then told her father so the terrace was locked.

qa.q: How might the two friends who walked Hafsa down have seen her choice?
qa.a: They may have respected it, or felt relieved themselves, since they chose to leave the chanting and go with her.

grounding: Shows, in an elder's memory, a teenager who feels most alive in a crowd and says yes to everything, until the pull to please nearly leads her into danger.

passage: By Saturday afternoon Yusuf had said yes to three things: cricket at four, Sachin's science model at five, Farah's birthday at six. He had never been good at no. At the ground, some older boys were heading to the lake on their bikes. 'Come, Yusuf, you're fun.' He felt the warm rush of being wanted, and went, his phone buzzing in his pocket. At the lake they dared each other to jump off the old jetty; Yusuf laughed along but stayed on the planks, suddenly unsure. When he checked his phone it was seven: four missed calls from Sachin and a photo of a half-built model. He had missed the birthday too. At home that night, alone, the house felt flat and grey. He typed 'sorry' to Sachin, deleted it, and typed it again.

qa.q: What had Yusuf said yes to for Saturday?
qa.a: Cricket at four, Sachin's science model at five and Farah's birthday at six.

qa.q: What did Yusuf feel when the older boys said 'you're fun'?
qa.a: He felt a warm rush of being wanted, which pulled him along even though he had promised Sachin.

qa.q: What could Yusuf try before saying yes next time?
qa.a: Check what he has already promised and say 'not today' to new plans, keeping his word to friends like Sachin.

qa.q: What was Saturday like for Sachin?
qa.a: Sachin was left building the model alone, calling four times, probably hurt and let down.

grounding: Shows a teenager who says yes to every plan and feels flat alone, whose need for company slides into letting a friend down and drifting toward risk.

passage: The flat in Madhapur went silent after his parents left for a wedding in Vizag, and within an hour Naveen felt like a phone on two percent. He messaged six people. Zainab replied first: 'Studying, sorry! Tomorrow?' The only yes came from the seniors' group: 'Come over. Bring your laptop.' He went, and it was loud and bright, and he felt alive again. Around ten one of them said, 'Naveen, you're good at essays, na? Do ours for Monday? You're one of us now.' Everyone looked at him. He heard himself say, 'Sure, no problem.' Walking home, the glow faded. Three essays, and his own not started. Zainab called. 'Why do you sound weird?' He told her. 'Would they still invite you if you said no?' she asked. He didn't know. That was the worst part.

qa.q: What did the seniors ask Naveen to do?
qa.a: Write their essays for Monday.

qa.q: Why did Naveen say 'Sure, no problem'?
qa.a: He felt alive and wanted in the group, and was afraid that saying no would cost him that belonging.

qa.q: What could Naveen say to the seniors now?
qa.a: He could tell them honestly that he won't write their essays, and find out whether they still invite him, as Zainab's question suggests.

qa.q: How might Zainab feel hearing Naveen's story?
qa.a: Zainab seems concerned for him, asking a gentle question so he sees the cost of saying yes to everything.

grounding: Shows a teenager who feels flat alone and alive in a crowd, and whose need for company slides into peer-pleasing.

passage:
Monday
Group presentation today. Five minutes of talking and I felt like I'd run a marathon. Payal did the intro, I did the data slides. Afterwards everyone went to the canteen and I came straight home and lay on my bed under the fan for an hour. Ammi knocked twice. 'Are you upset? You never talk any more.' I'm not upset. I'm just empty after people. And Sehar told someone I'm 'too proud to talk'. That stung. I'm not proud. I think before I speak, and by the time I've thought, the conversation has moved on. Payal texted at eight: 'You were great. Chai tomorrow, just us?' That's why she's my best friend. She never needs me to be loud.
Rehana

qa.q: What did Rehana do in the group presentation?
qa.a: The data slides.

qa.q: How did Rehana feel on hearing about the 'too proud to talk' comment?
qa.a: Rehana felt stung and misunderstood, not proud at all, just someone who thinks before speaking.

qa.q: How could Rehana answer Ammi's worry?
qa.a: By explaining that time alone after school is how Rehana recharges, not a sign of being upset, and maybe suggesting a quiet chat later.

qa.q: Why does Payal's text matter so much to Rehana?
qa.a: Payal praises Rehana and offers chai for just the two of them, a loyal friend who never needs Rehana to be loud.

grounding: Shows a teenager who is drained by a group presentation, recharges alone, is mistaken for proud, and has a deep, loyal friendship.

passage:
Vandana: party at Sid's tonight, u coming?
Nikita: can't today

qa.q: What might Nikita have felt reading 'ppl think ur a snob'?
qa.a: Nikita probably felt hurt and misunderstood, replying only 'oh' before explaining.

qa.q: What did Nikita do that helped Vandana understand?
qa.a: Nikita explained honestly about needing time alone to recharge and offered a one-to-one movie, showing it isn't coldness.

qa.q: How does Vandana's view of Nikita change during the chat?

passage: Every day after school in their village near Bikaner, Neelam climbed to the roof with her notebook and stayed there till the cows came home. Her brother Nilesh called her 'the queen upstairs'. At the youth meeting in the panchayat hall that week, everyone argued loudly about the new water tank. Neelam sat silent for an hour. Then, near the end, she raised her hand. 'If the tank goes by the temple, the families in the lower basti will walk twice as far. Can it go in between?' The hall went quiet. The sarpanch wrote it down. Walking home, Nilesh kicked a stone. 'Where did that come from?' 'From the roof,' she said. 'I think better up there.' That evening her friend Kiran came with two cups of chai, and they sat on the roof together, hardly talking, the way they had since Class 2.

qa.q: What did Neelam suggest about the water tank?
qa.a: That it go in between, so the families in the lower basti wouldn't walk twice as far.

qa.q: How might Neelam have felt sitting silent for an hour at the meeting?
qa.a: She was probably calm and absorbed, thinking carefully before speaking, rather than bored or aloof.

qa.q: What could Nilesh learn from the meeting?
qa.a: That Neelam's time alone on the roof is where her ideas form, so calling her 'the queen upstairs' misreads her.

qa.q: How might Kiran see Neelam?
qa.a: Kiran, a friend since Class 2, sees a loyal, easy companion to share quiet chai with, not someone aloof.

grounding: Shows a teenager who recharges alone, thinks before speaking and is mistaken for aloof, yet offers a deep idea and keeps a long, loyal friendship.

passage:
Dear Swati,
The whole gang asked me to write this, because I'm the one who writes long messages.
We noticed you left the fair early two weekends in a row, and on Friday you looked like you were holding your face up with both hands. We think we've been dragging you to everything loud because that's what Karan and I like. That isn't fair.
So here's the new plan. First Saturday of the month: something loud, the fair, cricket, whatever. Third Sunday: a quiet one, the library café or a walk by the lake. You can come to both, one or neither, and nobody will sulk.
And one question, which you can answer later, not now: how much of us do you want in a week? Honestly. We'd rather know than guess.
Shankar

qa.q: What is planned for the third Sunday?
qa.a: A quiet one, the library café or a walk by the lake.

qa.q: What did Shankar and the gang feel when they noticed Swati leaving early?
qa.a: They felt concerned and a bit guilty, realising they had dragged Swati to everything loud because that's what some of them liked.

qa.q: Why is the question 'how much of us do you want in a week?' wise?
qa.a: It lets Swati say what suits, so the group can avoid both leaving Swati lonely and wearing Swati out.

qa.q: How might Swati feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Swati would probably feel relieved and cared for, free to choose without anyone sulking.

grounding: Shows a friend group that plans both loud and quiet outings and asks a tired friend how much company they want.

passage: So there are six of us, right? I'm Imran, the loud one, obviously. Last year we did the same thing every Saturday: the arcade, then pav bhaji at the beach, then someone's terrace till midnight. I loved it. I thought everyone loved it. Then Chaitanya started 'having a headache' every Saturday. I got annoyed, honestly. I thought he'd found better friends. So one day, walking back from tuition, I just asked him: 'How much of us do you actually want?' He went quiet, and then he said, 'Maybe one big thing a week, and one small thing. Saturdays are a lot.' So now we alternate. Loud Saturday, then chess and chai at his place the next week. And guess what? I like the chess weeks too. And Chaitanya comes to every loud Saturday now, because he isn't dreading it.

qa.q: What did Chaitanya suggest?
qa.a: One big thing a week and one small thing.

qa.q: How did Imran feel when Chaitanya kept 'having a headache'?
qa.a: Imran felt annoyed and a bit hurt, worried that Chaitanya had found better friends.

qa.q: What did Imran's question on the walk back achieve?
qa.a: It got Chaitanya to say plainly how much company suited him, which led to alternating loud and quiet weeks.

qa.q: What were those Saturdays like for Chaitanya before the change?
qa.a: They were too much; Chaitanya dreaded them and made excuses rather than risk upsetting the group.

grounding: Shows a friend group that learns to ask a quieter friend how much company he wants, and alternates loud and quiet outings.

passage: I sit behind Preeti and Urmila in Class 11, so I hear most things. After the practicals, the whole group was planning the Diwali mela: rides, crowds, the works. Urmila was quiet, rubbing her eyes. Most groups would have said, 'Come on, don't be boring.' I've said that myself. Preeti didn't. She turned round and asked, low, 'Big crowd today, or small?' Urmila said, 'Small. Sorry.' 'Don't be sorry.' Then Preeti told the others to go ahead, said she'd have jalebi with Urmila at the corner shop instead, and they'd all do the mela on Saturday. Nobody sulked. On Saturday Urmila was at the mela, laughing on the giant wheel. I don't know what goes on in their heads. But I've noticed I've started asking my own friends that question.

qa.q: What question did Preeti ask Urmila?
qa.a: 'Big crowd today, or small?'

qa.q: What might Urmila have been feeling when she said 'Small. Sorry.'?
qa.a: Urmila was probably tired and a little guilty, worried about spoiling the group's plan.

qa.q: What did Preeti's approach get right?
qa.a: She asked instead of pushing, let the others go ahead, and stayed with Urmila, so nobody was left lonely or worn out.

qa.q: How has watching this changed the narrator?
qa.a: The narrator, who used to say 'don't be boring', now asks friends how much company they want.

grounding: Shows, through a classmate's account, a friend who asks a tired friend how much company she wants and splits the plan instead of pushing her.

passage:
'You're not going to the alumni dinner?' Tanvir's voice crackled over the phone. 'Ira, the whole batch will be there.'
'I did three interviews today, Bhaiya. And the pre-placement talk. I smiled for nine hours.'
'And?'
'And I was good. Two shortlists.' She lay flat on the hostel bed. 'Now my face hurts and I need the lights off.'
'You used to feel guilty saying no to anything.'
'I still do, a bit. But I picked. There's one alumna from the data team I actually want to talk to. I've emailed her for coffee on Saturday. Just her.'
'Instead of forty people.'
'Instead of forty people I'd forget by Monday.'
Tanvir laughed. 'Okay. Lights off, then. Proud of you.'
'Thanks.' She was already pulling the blanket over her head.

qa.q: How many shortlists did Ira get?
qa.a: Two.

qa.q: How did Ira feel after the day of interviews?
qa.a: Ira felt drained, her face aching from smiling, and still a little guilty about saying no to the dinner.

qa.q: Why is Ira's coffee plan a good choice?
qa.a: It trades forty forgettable chats for one meaningful conversation with someone she really wants to meet, after she has recharged.

qa.q: How does Tanvir see Ira's decision by the end of the call?
qa.a: Tanvir moves from teasing to understanding and ends up proud of her.

grounding: Shows a young adult who performs well at interviews but needs quiet afterwards, and chooses one meaningful conversation over a crowded dinner.

passage: At the first job fair of my final year, I tried to talk to every stall. Twenty-two companies in five hours. I'm Tejas, and I'm actually decent at these things: I can smile, crack a joke, pitch my project in ninety seconds. People told me I was a natural. Then I got back to the hostel and couldn't speak for the rest of the night. My roommate thought I'd had bad news. I hadn't. I was just empty. Before the second fair, Hafsa, a senior who'd been through it, told me to pick four stalls and go deep. I felt guilty walking past the others, as if I were throwing away chances. But the four conversations were real, and one turned into an internship. That evening I still needed my room and silence, but for an hour, not a whole night.

qa.q: How many companies did Tejas visit at the first job fair?
qa.a: Twenty-two.

qa.q: How did Tejas feel walking past the other stalls at the second fair?
qa.a: Tejas felt guilty, as if throwing away chances, even while following Hafsa's advice.

qa.q: What made Hafsa's advice work for Tejas?
qa.a: Choosing four stalls meant fewer but real conversations, one became an internship, and Tejas needed far less time to recover.

qa.q: How might Tejas's roommate have read that first silent night?
qa.a: The roommate thought Tejas had had bad news, mistaking tiredness after people for something wrong.

grounding: Shows a young adult who shines at a job fair but is drained afterwards, and learns to choose a few meaningful conversations despite feeling guilty.

passage:
Supervisor's note, week 3, intern: Vishal
Vishal ran the demo table at Thursday's launch and was excellent: clear, warm, patient with every question for four hours. Several clients asked who he was. On Friday morning he asked me, a little awkwardly, if he could work from the quiet room and skip the team lunch. My first reaction was that he seemed ungrateful. I asked him about it instead. He said events use up everything he has, and he needs a stretch of quiet to think properly again. He also said he feels guilty turning down invitations. We agreed: after big events a quiet morning is fine, and he will choose one or two client follow-ups rather than all eleven. His follow-up emails on Friday were the most thoughtful of the batch.
Gurleen

qa.q: How long did Vishal run the demo table?
qa.a: For four hours.

qa.q: What does Vishal feel about turning down invitations?
qa.a: He feels guilty, even though he knows he needs quiet after events.

qa.q: What did Gurleen and Vishal agree, and why is it sensible?
qa.a: A quiet morning after big events and one or two chosen client follow-ups instead of all eleven; it lets him recover and put his energy where it counts.

qa.q: What might have happened if Gurleen had acted on that first reaction?
qa.a: Gurleen might have judged Vishal ungrateful and pushed him into the lunch, leaving him drained and his follow-ups less thoughtful.

grounding: Shows, in a supervisor's note, a young adult who performs well at an event but needs quiet afterwards, and learns to choose a few follow-ups without guilt.

passage: In the Monday meeting at the logistics office in Gurgaon, the loud voices filled every gap. Ramesh had a thought about the delayed trucks, turned it over, checked it, and by the time he was sure, the discussion had moved on. That night he wrote it up in a tidy email: route the Jaipur loads through the Rewari depot on Tuesdays, when it sat empty. No reply. On Thursday a colleague said nearly the same thing in the meeting and got applause. Ramesh's jaw tightened. The next Monday he tried something small. At the start he said, 'Can I take two minutes at the end for one point?' Saurabh, the manager, nodded, a little surprised. Ramesh used them to walk through the numbers. Afterwards Saurabh stopped at his desk. 'Send me anything like this before meetings. And I'll ask you last, not first.'

qa.q: Which depot did Ramesh suggest for the Jaipur loads?
qa.a: The Rewari depot, on Tuesdays when it sat empty.

qa.q: What did Ramesh feel when a colleague got applause for nearly his idea?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and overlooked, his jaw tightening.

qa.q: What small opening did Ramesh create, and why did it work?
qa.a: He asked at the start for two minutes at the end, which gave him a guaranteed slot and time to prepare instead of fighting for a gap.

qa.q: How did Saurabh's view of Ramesh change?
qa.a: Saurabh, surprised at first, saw the value of Ramesh's careful thinking and offered to take his input before meetings and ask him last.

grounding: Shows a quiet young professional whose written idea is overlooked until he sets up a small opening to speak, and a manager who then asks for his input.

passage:
'Arohi, got a minute?' Rashmi closed the cabin door. 'Your write-up on the checkout screen. Where did that come from?'
'I noticed people drop off at the address page. I tested it on six people over the weekend.'
'It's brilliant. Why didn't you say any of it in Tuesday's review?'
Arohi looked at her hands. 'By the time I've thought it through, the meeting's on the next slide. And everyone talks so fast.'
'So your best ideas reach my inbox two days late.'
'Sorry.'
'Don't be sorry. Be early. What if I send the agenda a day ahead and you post one line in the chat before we start?'
'I can do that.'
'And in the meeting I'll say, Arohi, anything from your note? You say one thing. Deal?'
Arohi smiled, a little nervous. 'One thing. Deal.'

qa.q: Where did Arohi notice people dropping off?
qa.a: At the address page.

qa.q: What does Arohi looking at her hands suggest she feels?
qa.a: She feels a little embarrassed and uneasy, as if caught out for not speaking up.

qa.q: Why might Rashmi's plan work for Arohi?
qa.a: It gives Arohi thinking time with the agenda a day early, a written line to start with, and a guaranteed small opening to speak.

qa.q: How does Rashmi seem to see Arohi's quietness?
qa.a: Rashmi sees it as a timing problem, not a lack of ideas, and values the write-up enough to change how meetings run.

grounding: Shows a quiet young professional who shares best in writing, and a manager who creates small openings for her to speak.

passage: In my first year at the NGO, I was sure my manager thought I had nothing to say. I'm Dilnaz, and in meetings I was the one taking notes while everyone else talked over each other. I'd have an idea, and by the time I'd turned it over twice, someone louder had moved on. My ideas lived in my notebook. What changed wasn't me becoming loud. It was Santosh, my manager, who started ending each meeting with, 'Anything anyone wants to add by email tonight?' That night I sent three paragraphs on why our survey was missing the women who worked night shifts. He read it out the next morning and put me in charge of fixing it. I still don't jump into arguments. But I've learnt to say, early, 'I'll send a note on this,' and people wait for it now.

qa.q: What did Dilnaz's three paragraphs point out?
qa.a: That the survey was missing the women who worked night shifts.

qa.q: How did Dilnaz feel in those early meetings?
qa.a: Dilnaz felt overlooked and frustrated, sure the manager thought Dilnaz had nothing to say.

qa.q: What small opening has Dilnaz learned to create?
qa.a: Saying early, 'I'll send a note on this,' so people know a written point is coming and wait for it.

qa.q: What did Santosh gain by asking for input by email?
qa.a: He heard careful ideas that got lost in loud meetings, like the survey gap, and found the right person to fix it.

grounding: Shows a quiet young professional whose written ideas are overlooked in loud meetings until a manager asks for input later and sees their value.

passage:
'Harish is crying, Joseph. His truck broke.'
Joseph looked at his own red truck, then toddled over and pushed it into Harish's hands. He patted Harish's head. 'There. There.'
'That's kind, kanna,' said Amma. 'Can you bring me the spoon?'
Joseph fetched it, beaming.
Later Amma saw him watching Harish zoom the red truck, his thumb in his mouth.
'Joseph, did you want to keep your truck?'
Joseph's chin wobbled. 'Mine. Also.'
'Then after lunch it comes back to you.'

qa.q: What did Joseph give Harish?
qa.a: His red truck.

qa.q: What does Joseph's thumb in his mouth, watching Harish, suggest?
qa.a: He may be feeling a little sad and missing his truck, a want he didn't say out loud.

qa.q: Why was Amma's question a good idea?
qa.a: It let Joseph say he wanted his truck too, so his kindness didn't hide his own wish, and a turn after lunch made it fair.

qa.q: How might Harish feel when Joseph pats his head?
qa.a: Harish probably feels comforted, getting a truck and a pat just when his own toy broke.

grounding: Shows a toddler who warmly hands over a toy, comforts a crying child and follows requests, while hiding a want an adult asks about.

passage:
Note for Omkar's parents
Omkar was our little helper today. When Tia cried for her mother, he brought her his blanket and patted her back. He put the blocks away when asked. At snack he gave his biscuit to Rayan. Ten minutes later I found him by the window, eyes wet. I asked, 'Did you want your biscuit?' He nodded. We shared mine. He gives so quickly that he may not say what he wants, so I'll keep checking.
Afreen, caregiver

qa.q: What did Omkar bring Tia?
qa.a: His blanket.

qa.q: Why were Omkar's eyes wet by the window?
qa.a: He was sad about giving away his biscuit; he had wanted it but hadn't said so.

qa.q: What is Afreen's plan, and why does it matter?
qa.a: To keep checking what Omkar wants, because he gives so quickly that his own wishes can go unspoken.

qa.q: How might Omkar's parents feel reading this note?
qa.a: Proud of his kindness, and glad the caregiver noticed his hidden want and gently asked.

grounding: Shows, in a caregiver's note, a toddler who comforts and shares readily and follows requests, but hides his own want until an adult asks.

passage: At the village feast in Goa, Francis followed his mother Sarita everywhere, proudly carrying her basket of bananas when she asked. When a little girl dropped her sweet in the dust and wailed, Francis toddled over and held out his own. Then he stood by the rope swing, watching the bigger children, not asking. Sarita crouched. 'Do you want a turn, baba?' He nodded hard. She lifted him on and pushed him gently.

qa.q: What did Francis carry for Sarita?
qa.a: Her basket of bananas.

qa.q: What does Francis standing by the swing, not asking, suggest?
qa.a: He wanted a turn but stayed quiet, perhaps shy, so his wish was hidden.

qa.q: What did Sarita's question do for Francis?
qa.a: It brought out the want he hadn't said, so he got his turn on the swing.

qa.q: How might the little girl feel when Francis holds out his sweet?
qa.a: She would likely feel comforted and surprised, her tears easing at an unexpected kindness.

grounding: Shows a toddler who happily follows requests and comforts a crying child, while a quiet want goes unspoken until his mother asks.

passage: At his cousin's birthday in their Pune society hall, Lokesh took one bite of cake and announced, 'This is too sweet. I don't like it.' The aunty who baked it laughed awkwardly. Later, when two big boys pushed to the front of the game line, Lokesh planted his feet. 'No. There's a line. Go back.' They went back. Walking home, his papa Vikas said, 'You were right about the line. Strong.' Lokesh grinned. 'And the cake?' 'True, maybe. But Aunty worked hard. You could say, thank you, it's very sweet for me.' 'Still true?' 'Still true. Just kinder.'

qa.q: What did Lokesh say about the cake?
qa.a: 'This is too sweet. I don't like it.'

qa.q: What does Lokesh planting his feet in the line show?
qa.a: He felt determined and sure about fairness, not scared of the big boys.

qa.q: How did Vikas guide Lokesh?
qa.a: He praised the honesty about the line and showed a kinder way to say the truth about the cake: 'thank you, it's very sweet for me.'

qa.q: How might the aunty who baked the cake have felt?
qa.a: She probably felt a bit hurt or embarrassed, laughing awkwardly at the blunt remark.

grounding: Shows a young child who says exactly what he thinks and stands up for fairness, and a parent guiding him toward a kinder tone.

passage:
'Dhruv took four green and I only got one. That's not fair!'
'I needed green for my tree,' Dhruv said.
'I need green for my frog. You're greedy.'
Mumma looked up. 'Nandini.'
'He is! I'm just saying the truth.'
'You're right that it isn't fair. Greedy is a hurting word, though. Try again.'
Nandini scowled, then folded her arms. 'Dhruv. Please give me two green. Then we're equal.'
Dhruv slid two across. 'Fine.'
'Thank you,' Nandini said, still scowling a little. 'Now my frog can be green.'

qa.q: How many green crayons did Dhruv take?
qa.a: Four.

qa.q: What was Nandini feeling when she called Dhruv greedy?
qa.a: She felt angry and certain it was unfair, and determined to say so.

qa.q: What did Mumma get right?
qa.a: She agreed it wasn't fair but asked for a kinder word, so Nandini kept her honesty and changed her tone.

qa.q: How might Dhruv feel being called greedy?
qa.a: Dhruv probably felt stung and defensive, since he did need green for his tree.

grounding: Shows a young child who argues bluntly for fairness and won't give way, and a parent guiding her toward a kinder tone.

passage:
Note to Vasudha's parents
Vasudha had a strong day. When our visiting artist showed a cat drawing, Vasudha said loudly, 'That looks like a dog.' Some children giggled and the moment went flat. At snack time she noticed the boys' table had more fruit and told our helper, 'That's not fair. Count them.' She was right, and would not sit until it was fixed. I told her I was proud she spoke up. We also practised 'I think' instead of 'That is'. Her honesty is a gift; we're working on her tone.
Sharmila, class teacher

qa.q: What did Vasudha notice at snack time?
qa.a: That the boys' table had more fruit.

qa.q: What does Vasudha refusing to sit until the fruit was fixed show?
qa.a: She felt strongly about fairness and was determined, not willing to give way.

qa.q: How does the 'I think' practice help Vasudha?
qa.a: It keeps her honest opinion but softens the tone, so she can say what she thinks more kindly.

qa.q: How might the visiting artist have felt?
qa.a: The artist may have felt a little awkward and deflated as the children giggled and the moment went flat.

grounding: Shows, in a teacher's note, a young child who speaks bluntly and argues for fairness, with an adult guiding her toward a kinder tone.

passage: In the colony park in Chennai, Minakshi always chose the game, and Gopika always said yes. Today it was hide-and-seek again, which Gopika hated: the dark corner behind the watchman's cabin made her stomach tight. She hid there anyway. Later Minakshi's ball smashed Mrs. Rao's flowerpot. Mrs. Rao came out, furious. 'Who did this?' Minakshi went pale. 'I did,' Gopika said quickly. 'Sorry, Aunty.' At home, Amma had already heard from Mrs. Rao. 'Why did you say it was you?' Gopika's eyes filled. 'Minakshi would cry. Then nobody would play.' Amma sat beside her. 'If you tell the truth, or say no to hide-and-seek, will Minakshi stop being your friend?' Gopika didn't know. That scared her most.

qa.q: Whose flowerpot did the ball smash?
qa.a: Mrs. Rao's.

qa.q: Why did Gopika say 'I did'?
qa.a: She was anxious about conflict; if Minakshi cried nobody would play, and she only feels safe when everyone is happy.

qa.q: How could Amma help Gopika after this?
qa.a: Help her practise small, kind 'no's and telling the truth, and show her that friends usually stay even when she disagrees.

qa.q: How might Minakshi feel about Gopika taking the blame?
qa.a: Minakshi was probably relieved at first, but may also feel uneasy or guilty that Gopika took the blame for Minakshi's ball.

grounding: Shows a child who agrees to games she dislikes and takes the blame to avoid conflict, and a parent beginning to help her see that no won't end a friendship.

passage:
'You look tired, Gopu.'
'I played teacher-teacher with Rinku again. I'm always the student who gets scolded.'
'Do you like being the student?'
'No. I like drawing.' Gopika picked at the sofa. 'But Rinku gets upset if I say no. Then she won't talk to me.'
'For how long?'
Gopika thought. 'Last time, till lunch.'
'And then?'
'Then she wanted to sit with me.'
'So a no costs you one morning, and she still comes back.' Vidya grinned. 'Let's practise. I'm Rinku. Gopika, come play teacher-teacher!'
Gopika giggled, then took a breath. 'Not today. I want to draw. Tomorrow I'll play.'
'Hmph,' said Vidya-as-Rinku. 'Okay. Can I watch you draw?'
'Rinku wouldn't say that.'
'Try it and see.'

qa.q: What does Gopika like doing instead of playing teacher-teacher?
qa.a: Drawing.

qa.q: What is Gopika afraid will happen if she says no to Rinku?
qa.a: She is anxious that Rinku will get upset and stop talking to her.

qa.q: How did Vidya help Gopika see that saying no is safe?
qa.a: By asking what happened last time, Rinku sulked till lunch and then came back, and by letting her practise a kind no.

qa.q: Why might Rinku react differently from how Gopika fears?
qa.a: Last time Rinku only sulked till lunch and then wanted to sit with Gopika, so the friendship may be sturdier than Gopika thinks.

grounding: Shows a child who keeps agreeing to a game she dislikes to keep a friend happy, and an older person helping her practise saying no.

passage: Last year I was the peacemaker of 6B. I'm Darshan. If two people fought over the class cricket bat, I gave up my turn. If the group wanted football, which I hate, I played goalkeeper and let everything in. When our science model fell off the desk, and it was really Rahul's elbow, I said it was me so Ma'am wouldn't shout at him. I only felt calm when everyone was smiling. Then Nazia, who sits next to me, said something that stuck: 'You know you're allowed to not want things, right?' I laughed. But the next week I told the group, 'I'll skip football today. I'm going to the library.' My heart was thumping. Nobody minded. Rahul still sat with me at lunch.

qa.q: What did Darshan tell the group the next week?
qa.a: 'I'll skip football today. I'm going to the library.'

qa.q: What was Darshan feeling when saying no to football?
qa.a: Darshan felt nervous, heart thumping, afraid that saying no would cost friendships.

qa.q: What helped Darshan start saying no?
qa.a: Nazia's remark that it's allowed to not want things, and then trying one small no and seeing that nothing broke.

qa.q: How might Rahul have felt when Darshan took the blame for his elbow?
qa.a: Rahul may have felt relieved to escape a scolding, but perhaps also guilty that Darshan paid for his mistake.

grounding: Shows a child who agrees to disliked games and takes the blame to keep the peace, and learns that saying no does not end friendships.

passage:
'So? Did you like my poem?'
'Honestly? The first half, yes. The ending's a greeting card.'
Gurpreet's face fell. 'Wow. Thanks, Ayesha.'
'You asked.'
'I asked if you liked it, not for a post-mortem.'
Ayesha opened her mouth, then shut it. 'Okay. That came out harsh. The first half really is good.'
That evening someone posted the class trip list in the group chat. Meher, the new girl, had been left off. 'She's weird,' someone wrote. Six laughing replies.
Ayesha typed: 'Put her back on. That's not fair and you know it.'
Silence. Then Gurpreet, still annoyed, messaged her privately: 'You're impossible. But you're right.'

qa.q: What did Ayesha say about the poem's ending?
qa.a: That it's a greeting card.

qa.q: What does Ayesha opening her mouth and then shutting it suggest?
qa.a: She realised she had hurt Gurpreet and felt a flicker of regret before softening her words.

qa.q: What could Ayesha keep, and what could she change, about her honesty?
qa.a: Keep speaking up against unfairness, as with the trip list; change the delivery of feedback by leading with what works.

qa.q: How does Gurpreet see Ayesha by the end of the day?
qa.a: Gurpreet is still stung about the poem but respects that Ayesha stood up for Meher: 'You're impossible. But you're right.'

grounding: Shows a teenager whose bluntness hurts a friend, and whose same honesty resists the group and speaks up against unfairness.

passage: In Class 11 I lost two friends in one week, and I'd do half of it again. I'm Dolma. I run the 800 metres, and I've never pretended I don't want to win. When Aparna beat me at districts, I told her straight: 'You ran smarter. I'm coming for you next time.' She laughed; we're still close. But then Coach picked the relay team from the ones who'd stayed back to help at his daughter's birthday, not the fastest. Everyone grumbled in the changing room. Only I said it to his face, calmly, with the timings on paper. Two teammates stopped talking to me; they said I'd made them look bad. Coach redid the trials. Maybe I could have said it in private first. That part I'd change. The rest, no.

qa.q: What did Dolma bring when speaking to Coach?
qa.a: The timings on paper.

qa.q: How does Dolma feel, looking back at that week?
qa.a: Dolma feels mostly sure speaking up was right, with a little regret about how and where it was said.

qa.q: What would Dolma change about raising the relay issue?
qa.a: Saying it to Coach in private first, while still using the timings to make a calm, fair case.

qa.q: Why might the two teammates have stopped talking to Dolma?
qa.a: They felt embarrassed and exposed, as if Dolma's challenge showed them going along with something unfair.

grounding: Shows a teenager who competes openly, doesn't need everyone's approval, and speaks up against an unfair selection at a cost to some friendships.

passage:
Class 10B, notes after the parent meeting: Vidya
Vidya is one of the most honest students I teach. In Tuesday's debate practice she told Karan, 'That argument is lazy. You didn't read the article.' She was not wrong, but he went red and didn't speak again. Afterwards I talked with her about saying the hard thing without the sting. She listened, arms folded, then said, 'Fine. But I won't pretend it was good.' Fair enough. The same week, when most of the class agreed to share answers for the online quiz, Vidya refused and told them why, in front of everyone. Nobody else did. Her parents worry she has no friends. I see a student who doesn't need permission to be fair. We agreed she'll start her feedback with one thing that works.
Ujjwal, class teacher

qa.q: What did Vidya say to Karan in debate practice?
qa.a: 'That argument is lazy. You didn't read the article.'

qa.q: What might Vidya have felt refusing to share quiz answers in front of everyone?
qa.a: She probably felt firm and determined, maybe uncomfortable, but not needing the class's approval to do what was fair.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal and Vidya agree, and why is it a good step?
qa.a: That she will start feedback with one thing that works; it keeps her honesty but lessens the sting for classmates like Karan.

qa.q: How might Karan have felt after Vidya's comment?
qa.a: Karan felt embarrassed, going red and staying silent for the rest of the practice.

grounding: Shows, in a teacher's note, a teenager whose blunt honesty can hurt but who also resists peer pressure and refuses to join in cheating.
